utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Call the case, please, Mr. Court deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-02-60-T, Vidoje Blagojevic and Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Before the cross-examination by Mr. Karnavas, is there anything that the parties would like to bring to the attention of this Bench? Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning. I wanted to ask permission from the Trial Chamber, in the cross-examination, I intend to use an exhibit which represents the model of the Zvornik Brigade headquarters from Zvornik in 1995, and so, as not to surprise the witness, at the break, I've spoken to security and they said they could take the model down to a cell to have him look at it or they could have it in the courtroom but I'd like him to have an opportunity to look at the model with his counsel before it's used in cross-examination today. If I could have your permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. We spoke about that. It seems fine. I would like to be present also. I don't need to -- shouldn't need to say anything but just would like to be present to see the model.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey is invited also, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So your application is permitted, is granted.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And I think this kind of practice should be encouraged, so that to save time during the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karnavas. Are you ready for the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, I am. Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we could pick up where we left off yesterday. We were talking a little bit about the -- on the 13th and going into the 14th, where you at the time had a lack of proper intelligence information with respect to the 28th Division. So I'm focusing you there. You had indicated, as I recall, that you had made -- you had placed a call to General Zivanovic, expressing your concerns, and also alerting him to this looming problem that was headed your way; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas. As I've already said, as I already told Mr. McCloskey, on the evening of the 13th, and I think the conversation was recorded, called General Zivanovic up and said that my ambush men had seen a column which was over three kilometres long.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I also showed you an order, if you recall, by the Drina Corps, asking the Bratunac Brigade, the Milici and Skelani Brigade to search the terrain. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And during this period of time, while you were making this phone call, alerting General Zivanovic, who at the time - correct me if I'm wrong - you believed to be the commander of the Drina Corps, your commander, Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic, was on a mission in the opposite direction, towards Zepa. Am I correct in stating that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, I showed you yesterday the Drina Corps' order dated July 2nd, 1995, upon which the Zvornik order was constructed, also dated July 2nd, 1995. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You showed us those papers yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And as I understand your testimony and correct me if I'm wrong - that when Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic drafted his order, he in essence, gave himself more of a role than was actually required of him under that particular order, and by that I mean he actually took almost two full battalions, or composed two full battalions, to head off for Srebrenica, whereas the order itself that came from the Drina Corps required a lesser role, a smaller unit, if we could term it -- put it in those terms. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Am I also not correct, Mr. Obrenovic, that Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic, when he went off to Srebrenica with those two, in essence, you know, battalions, one of which comprised of the Drina Wolves, is it not also a fact that he took a great deal of the resources, vital resources, from the Zvornik Brigade, communications, the best armament, the best equipment available to the Drina Corps, in order for him to have his, shall we say, A-team be engaged in this attack against Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, might I just make a brief explanation with that regard?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that in the written order signed by General Zivanovic, the Drina Corps to the Zvornik Brigade, it did state that he should set a column of the strength of about 400 men, which would be equivalent to a light brigade. But Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic formed a tactical group, and yesterday you showed us the order to that effect, and it was something Mr. McCloskey asked me about. That tactical group, according to his decision, had two combat groups. One combat group, as you rightly said, was the battalion of the Drina Wolves, or the Special Forces of the Drina Detachment of the Zvornik Brigade, and the second combat group, Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic set up by taking men from all our battalions and took an intervention platoon, making up two companies under the command of the 1st Battalion, Lieutenant Stanojevic. And you're quite right, he took all of the available men in the Zvornik Brigade important for battle. And it is also correct that there was artillery support, communications support, and an armoured, or rather a tank platoon and a plank of self-propelled canons. And it says this in the order. On the 3rd, in the morning, I made a remark to Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic - I'm not quite sure of the date. I think it was the morning of the 3rd - and I asked him what's the Zvornik Brigade going to defend itself with, the 2nd Corps of it? And he said that everything was within a radius of one hour's distance. And the 2nd Corps wouldn't be able to do anything significant anyway until the units returned. So it was with this idea that those forces were deployed towards Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if I can return slightly back to our conversation that we had yesterday with respect to the lines that were divided, the Republika Srpska from the BiH, where the 2nd Corps was and where the Zvornik Brigade was. Do you recall that conversation where you demonstrated on the map where the line was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I remember it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I want us to all try to visualise what was going on during those days. Prior to the attack on Srebrenica, and prior to the advancement of the 28th Division, would I be correct in stating that your forces, that is, the Zvornik Brigade forces, were facing, in essence, the 2nd Corps? In other words, you had the 2nd Corps looking at you, you, on the other hand, facing the 2nd Corps, and so that was your line of defence. Because in your rear was the Republika Srpska, and, of course, you didn't have to worry about the municipality of Zvornik, and across the Drina River you had Serbia; right? Am I correct? And I know I'm generalising a little bit.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In general terms, yes. Across from the Zvornik Brigade wasn't the entire 2nd Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but two of their divisions, if I remember correctly. I think it was the 24th and 25th, in actual fact. So not the entire corps, but significant forces, significant manpower, and the ratio was 1 and a half to 1, compared to us. We had a little more technical equipment, but they were far numerous compared to the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But if I could just make sure that I have it correctly. Your forces, though, were facing in that direction, towards the 2nd Corps, as they were facing you. That was where your troops had been stationed for quite a long time, years, in fact?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So now with the 28th Division coming up from the Srebrenica area, passing between the Milici and the Bratunac Brigade, would it be correct in stating that now your troops, the Zvornik Brigade, not only had to defend itself against the 2nd Corps, but now on their rear side, their backs or their sides, was coming the 28th, so now you more or less had a two-front defence, if I may put it in those sort of crude terms.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that that kind of battle is called a strike manoeuvre from the rear and that is one of the most difficult ways in which you can enter into combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it during -- as we indicated, Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic has taken quite a bit of the resources, he's taken some of the best fighting men, including the Drina Wolves, probably not anticipating anything of the sort would happen, and here you are now having to manoeuvre your troops so they can cover the 2nd Corps and also they have to manoeuvre around and be prepared for the advancing 28 Division, the numbers of which you are unclear of, all way up until perhaps as late as the 14th or the 15th?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I realise the situation was serious on the 13th, in the evening, when I saw the column that was three kilometres long. Then I realised that the strength of the column was far greater than the 300 that had been mentioned. And on the 14th, everything became absolutely clear with respect to the strength of the 28th Division. I saw it with my own eyes then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I think this set of questions has been asked yesterday, and I'm a little bit puzzled to see your point. I don't think there's any disputes, you know, on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: There isn't a dispute. However, Your Honour, I wanted to make it abundantly clear that the gentleman was facing two fronts at the same time, and the lines had been there for a long time, three years, and now his troops, which were reservists, were having to deal with a unique situation that they totally were unprepared for. But I will move on. That was the point I'm trying to make, because I'm trying to establish that based on Nikolic's testimony, where everything was copacetic as far as intelligence is concerned, now we're finding out, contrary to what Nikolic has stated, there was a great divide as far as knowledge with respect to where the 28th Division is and how large it is and how dangerous it proved to be later on. But I will move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, we talked -- we mentioned the Drina Wolves. Just so we all understand, could you give us a description of the Drina Wolves? Who were they?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, what do you want me to say? To describe them how? Their establishment or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What kind of a unit was it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Establishment-wise it was the equivalent of an infantry battalion, and within their composition they had the command for the detachment, or manoeuvre battalion, or whatever you like to call them, and as you called them, in fact, the Drina Wolves, which is what the people, local inhabitants called them. Then they had communication lines and two infantry companies, numbering 100 to 110 soldiers - I can't remember exactly now - and they also had a mixed mortar company for support, and it had 120 millimetres and 128-millimetre platoon mortars, and an armoured company with a tank platoon, T-55, and armoured transporters of the M-60 type, and if necessary, if they needed reinforcements, a Praga would be added, and a Praga platoon, and an engineers platoon. They would go with them to see to the mining and so on. Now, as to the basic weapons, I've already quoted some of the support weaponry. They were armed with light arms, automatic rifles of the standard Yugoslav-produced type. Of the protection devices, most of the infantry men had in the infantry companies helmets, I don't know exactly how many. I think they might have had 120 flak jackets, protective flak jackets, and all the necessary communication devices. They had a lot of combat experience. They were a very good combat unit, very well trained and capable. The command of the Drina Corps saw this detachment or battalion for what it was and used it frequently, and it would be out of Zvornik acting as a reserve for the Drina Corps. But it was within the composition of the Zvornik Brigade itself, in actual fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Can we conclude that it was -- that it was well known within the Drina Corps who this fighting unit was and their fighting capabilities? Did they have a reputation, in other words? That's what I'm trying to ...

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The corps commander knew that. It was a highly disciplined unit which listened to orders. It wasn't some sort of paramilitary unit, if that's what you had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No. No. No. Well, would other brigades, for instance, know of their reputation? Say, your neighbour, the Bratunac Brigade, would someone like the chief of intelligence and security know of the quality and fighting capabilities of the Drina Wolves, particularly given what you stated, that they were used outside the Zvornik area by the corps?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, it's difficult for me to say who knew what, but they could have known, yes. They had to have known.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Their commander was a gentleman by the name of -- or he had a nickname, Legenda. Is that -- am I correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At that time, Captain First Class Milan Jolovic, on the radio communication device, his code-name was Legenda, and so the nickname stuck, and people called him that. But that was his code-name for radio communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Was there a particular reason why they gave him this nickname?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't say. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. As I understand it, as some point General Krstic told you, on the 15th, that Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic was coming up and he was bringing up the Drina Wolves with him, and I take it hearing that must have brought you some relief, that help was finally on the way and that the help was of sufficient calibre to repel the attack or the battles with the 28th Division.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're quite right as far as the first part of your observation goes. It is true that I breathed a sigh of relief because the commander was coming in and I felt some relief because the battalion of the Drina Wolves was coming with the other units who were there. But I had no illusions that they would be able to do anything better. I knew that the 28th Division was a difficult thing to come up against.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. Now, and you had also requested help from the corps and at some point you did receive some help, albeit rather modest, from the Bratunac Brigade; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Already on the 14th, in the morning, I started entreating them for help through the radio devices and in my conversation with General Krstic. I asked that reinforcements be brought in. And the first reinforcements, the first help that came in, was a company of the civilian police, which came from Bijeljina. But Mane Djuric, Lieutenant Colonel, used it for the direct defence of Zvornik, contrary to my instructions. Now, around noon on the 15th, when I was attending a meeting with Borovcanin, Lieutenant Colonel Borovcanin, and Colonel Vasic, the first unit from Bratunac turned up. They arrived. They had come from the Bratunac Brigade. And somebody called me from the office, whether it was the duty officer or the assistant duty officer or whoever. I left the room and found three men standing there, some commanders, komandirs, standing there. That was the first unit that had arrived from Bratunac, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if I could show you what has been marked as D48 for identification purposes, and if you could kindly look at it. And it's a daily combat report prepared by the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade. And if you would look, just focus on more or less the first two paragraphs. The first paragraph, paragraph number 2. Just give that a quick glance. And I'm more interested in paragraph 2, the last part of that particular paragraph, where it describes some soldiers being sent.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read those two paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And would that be more or less consistent with your recollection of the events, what's in this particular daily combat report?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas. I told Mr. McCloskey 50 to 60 soldiers. It says 60 here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I didn't remember the exact figure, but they did arrive, probably around noon, 12.00. They arrived in Zvornik, or perhaps a little before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And that was on the 15th?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I think -- I believe, if I could just show you also what has been marked for identification purposes as P134. It's a -- the Prosecution has titled it: "Barrack duty officer logbook". I believe this was shown to you yesterday. It's dated 15/16. And over here it seems to indicate it was 10.00 in the morning, and that would have been on the 15th. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, this is a copy of a page from the duty shift officers in the barracks for the 15th and 16th of July, 1995, and the man in charge was Cvijetin Micic. I don't see when this was written exactly. It might have been written during the day or perhaps even on the 16th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And then of course there's another one with that in this particular attachment. I think it's page 8 in the English version. And it's dated 16/17, and there it says 40 men who were not members of the Zvornik Brigade stayed overnight. Were those men the men from the Bratunac Brigade, by any chance? If you can recall, or if you know.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was a platoon. I remember about 30 men. Possibly it was 40, 30 or 40, anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And if I could show what has been marked as D49 for identification purposes. And if you could look at paragraph number 2, just the first part, the first sentence of that paragraph. And this is an interim combat report from the Zvornik Brigade, and it's dated 16 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Would it be possible to get the English on the ELMO so that this can be made more public?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, is this -- the hundred men that came from the Bratunac, is this -- are these the men that came on the 16th, the 15th, or are we talking about both days? Because I believe that there were two groups that came, one on the 15th and then, later on, on the 16th.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In paragraph 2, it says our forces, and then it goes on to say the Zvornik Infantry Brigade, a company of the Ministry of the Interior of a hundred men, two platoons from the Bratunac Infantry Brigade. I think that the hundred men refers to the MUP company. And then part of the military police platoon from the Eastern Bosnia Corps. Yes, you are right. Although it says here that there were two platoons, it was actually 50 to 60 who arrived. As I said, we see here that Colonel Blagojevic said 60. That was around the 15th around noon and they were sent to Baljkovica straight away. After the 16th, another platoon arrived; I don't know whether it had 30 or 40 men. It doesn't matter. But they spent the night at the Standard barracks, and on the following day they were joined to the group that had arrived on the 15th, after the fighting. And together with our R Battalion, they were deployed on the Zvornik-Crni Vrh Road.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's what I'm going to get to. Now, I take it when the troops arrived from the Bratunac Brigade and they check in with you, at that point I believe you indicated they are under your command. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The first group, 50 or 60 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: When the second group arrives as well, when they check in, can we assume that now they're under the command of the commander of the Zvornik Brigade, whoever is in command at that particular moment, be it the commander or the acting commander?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: There are several terms. There's acting commander, there's deputy commander, there's commander, and interchanging them as if they have no consequence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In this particular case they have no consequence because the gentleman, Mr. Obrenovic, was in fact in command. Now, we can ask him whether he was the deputy commander or the acting commander while Mr. -- Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic was away. But in essence, you know, my point is: When these troops check in with the Zvornik Brigade, be it on the 15th or the 16th, are they not under the command of whoever is commanding the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I'm going to use a technical term. Maybe you can help us out here. Subordination. All right. Were they subordinated, once they check in, they come under your command, are they subordinated to you? So help me out here.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, the first group that arrived on the 15th, at the time of their arrival, I was the deputy commander, and commanding that part of our units in Zvornik, they came under my command. The second group that we have just mentioned, which arrived on the 16th, the commander was already there, and he commanded both those men and the other units as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, a little more broader. Are those troops now from the Bratunac Brigade, are they subordinated to the Zvornik Brigade? Is that the correct term? And if not, help us out.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the ones we are talking about now. Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if you could help us out here a little bit. On the 15th, when they were under your command, that group, how did you position that unit from the Bratunac Brigade? Where did you position them and how did you use them? I guess that's what I'm trying to get at.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, as I have already described, with three of their commanding officers I had a meeting in the operations room of our brigade command, and one of them said that under orders from Colonel Blagojevic, he was putting them at our disposal. He told me how many of them there were, what weapons they had. And then I informed them, briefly, about the 28th Division, at least what I knew about it. I said that this was an enormous force divided into three groups, consisting of 2.000 men each, and that the most dangerous group was the one that was breaking through, that they were destroying everything in front of them. And I was sending them to Baljkovica, to the command of the 4th Battalion, and the acting commander there, because the commander was away, would give them their combat tasks in fighting the 28th Division. I assigned a courier to take them there, and that was it. Later, on the 15th, in the afternoon, when I came to the 4th Battalion in the Baljkovica area, I felt that the deputy commander had deployed them in a wrong way. He had made them face north, in the wrong direction. I altered his decision and I ordered that this unit be moved and that they take up positions above us on a hill at Baljkovica, facing the south-west. They grumbled, but they obeyed the order, and they took up those positions facing the 28th Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, just a very direct question: Did you ever order any of those men to commit any atrocities, anybody that came from the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Karnavas. I have just told you what orders I gave, and that was all. Perhaps in Baljkovica I may have issued additional orders about opening fire when the fighting began in the late evening of the 15th. Later on they switched off their radio sets and got lost in the woods and we thought they had been taken prisoner. We only found them on the 16th, in the evening. Until that point in time, we considered them missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I guess my question was, you know, you didn't task them to do anything improper?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I've already said I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, the second group, do you know how they were tasked by Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic, if they were tasked at all?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, what I know is that they were attached on the 17th, in the morning, to the first group in Orahovac, and then I helped in their deployment and the deployment of other units on the Zvornik-Crni Vrh road. Before that, I don't know what orders they received from Commander Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And again, the tasks that at least you were involved with, were those proper military tasks, consistent with the situation on the ground and the request that you had made to the Bratunac Brigade pursuant to what had been happening between the Zvornik Brigade and the 28th Division?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, there are several questions here. First of all, I made no request of the Bratunac Brigade. My requests were sent to the corps command, and it was they who decided whether to send the Bratunac Brigade or somebody else. It was the Bratunac Brigade that turned up, so they sent them. As to the second part of your question, I repeat again: As for the two units from Bratunac, the first which arrived on the 15th, I gave them exclusively combat tasks, nothing criminal. The second unit which arrived on the 16th, I had nothing to do with them until they turned up in Orahovac on the 17th, and that was the first time I gave them concrete tasks about taking positions on that road. So again, it was a combat task I gave them, and nothing connected with any crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And I'm not insinuating that you did. I just want to make sure that I'm clear -- we have a clear record. Now, I want to turn our attention to what has been marked as P129 for identification purposes. We touched upon it a little bit yesterday, but I want to go into it a little bit more and try to put this matter to rest, if we can. P129. This is an intercept, and it's dated July 16, 1995. If you could look at it. I believe, Mr. President, that we may have an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The Defence for Mr. Jokic objects to the admission of any of the intercepts which were gathered by the OTP from the Army of the BiH. This represents one of those documents gathered from the Muslim army, and we believe that they are unreliable. Their reliability will be questioned completely. And therefore, it should be inadmissible. We just would like -- this is -- if one is allowed to be admissible, then they all would be allowed to be admissible, and our objection is that they -- none of the intercepts are admissible, due to lack of foundation and lack of reliability.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much to make your position once again very clearly, and I think we have made a ruling that at this stage we are not talking about the admission of the documents. We are talking about the using of these documents. Later on we'll discuss the matter whether those documents are admissible or not, depending on whether the Prosecution, I guess, is going to tender those documents into evidence or not. The admission, I think in the different jurisdictions has different meaning. Using the document, in my understanding, is not thought of as admission. But anyway, we'll bear in mind your objections, Ms. Sinatra. Mr. Karnavas, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the record, I don't intend to admit this, but I do wish the record to reflect that this was indeed admitted, or -- and relied upon in the Krstic judgement, at a time when perhaps there was some lack of clarity as far as one particular issue in this particular intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would debate the Krstic judgement and how it used that, Your Honour, so I don't think that's appropriate at this point, these sorts of comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I think the first part of your statement is relevant. You're informing us that this part of the document is admitted. I think that's enough. Here we are not sitting in Mr. Krstic's case, you know. There's no need. But of course if you have some doubts, if you have something that you want to clear up --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: -- You may do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Mr. Obrenovic, have you had a chance to look at it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, I'm primarily interested in discussing the issue with respect to anything coming from Blagojevic, anything being received from Blagojevic, that section of the intercept. And if I could just read it and then maybe we could have a little discussion. The question is: "Tell me, did anything arrive there now from Vidoje Blagojevic?" "From Vidoje?" "Today." "Yes... You mean manpower." "Yes, yes... Did anything arrive? Something was supposed to arrive." "Yes, it arrived... It's up there. It's up there, but it didn't arrive on time, and it wasn't brought in on time. And the others who arrived did arrive, but they were late, so they weren't brought in on time and that's why the commander who was here had problems." "When exactly did Blagojevic men arrive?" There's an expletive. "I don't know exactly, now I can't..." "I know the duty officer..." "Maybe the duty officer... Here's the duty officer." "Let me talk to him." And then it goes on. Now, I'm particularly interested in the phrase "up there." "It arrived -- it's up there." Now, as I understand it, as I understand it, in the context in which this is being referred to, up there doesn't mean north, does it, as in Pilica?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you expect me to give you my opinion, my interpretation of what Lieutenant Colonel Popovic meant by this, I've already stated my opinion. I think he's referring to Baljkovica on the area of the 4th Battalion, where the fighting was taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Is that up on a hill? Is that up there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: When you say "up there," isn't that the way that you would say it in Srpski to refer to up there meaning the hill up there where the fighting was going on? Is that as opposed to up there meaning in a direction of north?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas. "Up there" means the hill in Baljkovica. If he had wanted to mention Pilica, he would have said "down there," because the Drina flows downwards towards Pilica. In my view, he's suggesting "up there," meaning Baljkovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And as far as you know, as far as you recollect, were any men sent by you or Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic to Pilica at any time to participate in anything that went on there on that particular day?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I didn't send anyone to Pilica. Whether Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic sent anyone there, I wouldn't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Secondly, I was entreating them to send reinforcements and to send him back. That would have been completely illogical. I don't know why he said that. He may have been mistaken in the date. I don't know. I can't interpret his view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that this is one of the witnesses that was marked as P141, as we discussed the other day with Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You mean that he's a protected witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll have that part redacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I apologise. I wasn't aware that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I want to focus our attention to the night of the 13th, and in particular, the situation with Drago Nikolic and yourself, okay? As I understand it, sometime late in the evening on the 13th, you receive a call from Drago Nikolic from where he was stationed, and I think he was in the forward command post, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was on duty at Kitovnica, the forward command post there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And where were you when you received the call? Were you in the command post?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas. I was in my office, the office of the Chief of Staff in the command of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And this conversation took place -- I'm drawing a blank right now. What was the exact -- what was the time about when he called you? Was it 8.00 or 9.00, somewhere around there? I just don't recall right now.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said it was on the 13th, in the evening, but it's hard to determine the exact time. Probably between 1900 and 2000 hours. In any case, before I called General Zivanovic about the column. A little while after this, I called Zivanovic to tell him we saw a big column. So that can be a point in time that we could use for orientation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, as I understand it, he initially informs you of part of the message that he's received from Lieutenant Colonel Popovic of the Drina Corps security sector, or security organ. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, he told me that he had just received a call from Lieutenant Colonel Popovic. He didn't tell me he had called him from the Drina Corps command, or where he had called him from. He just told me that he had received a call from Lieutenant Colonel Popovic, and of course I knew what duty Popovic was performing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And but initially, he didn't tell you anything about -- well, initially, as I understand your testimony, he just said that Popovic had informed him that large numbers of prisoners would be heading your way into Zvornik. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that they would be heading, but that they would be brought there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. They would be brought there. All right. And upon hearing that news, particularly given the situation on the ground, that's when you reacted by questioning him about this information; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have already explained this to Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm trying to lay the groundwork, you know. Just "polako, polako." All right. So now, and when you press him, that's when he, as I understand it, Nikolic tells you that the decision has been -- a decision was made or an order, or Mladic issued the order to kill all of them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And he also says that everyone knows about it, including the commander?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I take it this was a rather brief conversation.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was brief, yes. It just consisted of what I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, before we dissect that information, let's talk a little bit about what was happening with you. You had been up for quite some time, had you not, the 11th, the 12th -- or the 12th and the 13th? So can we say -- is it fair to say that by this point of the day or the evening on the 13th, you were somewhat fatigued, tired, sleep deprived?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. To be quite precise, on the 12th I was woken up early in the morning. I didn't sleep a wink the night between the 12th and the 13th, and I've already mentioned that I had been on sick leave and that I was still limping. I was already exhausted then, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And apparently, after hearing this news, you didn't contact your own commander to try to check out this information that you had received. I'm wondering, might it be because of the fatigue factor, along with perhaps Nikolic's representation that Mladic had issued the order?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objecting to the multiple-part question, Your Honour. This is an important area and -- the witness should not have to dissect each part of a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, with all due respect to Mr. McCloskey, the gentleman, Mr. Obrenovic, seems to be doing quite well. But I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think it's obvious you could split your question into two parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I will do that. I'm trying to be efficient, Your Honour, but obviously I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: The most efficient way is to ask a very short and direct question to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right, Your Honour. I'll try that method. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: After receiving the call -- or during the call, you did not ask Nikolic whether he had in fact spoken with anyone else to verify the information that he was receiving from Lieutenant Colonel Popovic, did you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not ask him whether he had talked to anyone else, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And after hearing that information, you did not contact Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic to check out that information to see whether in fact that was correct, that is, that everybody knows, including the commander part?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right. I didn't. I didn't call Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic. I believed Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You didn't call -- well, when you did call General Zivanovic, who at the time you believed would still be the commander of the Drina Corps, you did not question him about this information that you had received from your lieutenant, I think first class, Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a lieutenant first class, and I did not inform General Zivanovic about what Nikolic had told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that -- I don't know what the reason is. It could be fatigue. But it seems to be that you did nothing to verify whether in fact the information that Nikolic was giving you and I'm particularly focusing on that everybody knows, including the commander part - that that information was true, accurate, and complete?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And so as you sit here today, there's nothing concretely that you can point out to that would at least give us some indication that Popovic did in fact tell Nikolic that everybody knows, including your commander? There's nothing that we can point to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, except for the fact what Drago Nikolic told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And -- well, we do know one thing about Drago Nikolic. As the days would progress, he proved to be a rather enthusiastic participant in the events.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. There's no sense in trying to help him out. And so there's no way of knowing whether that part of the information that Nikolic was giving you wasn't in fact something that he had made up, given that he seemed, at least in retrospect now, to have this predilection, this predisposition, against Muslims?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would request that the last remark by Mr. Karnavas be struck from the record. We don't -- this witness is here to tell the truth, not to help someone out or, as the inference may be left, to harm someone. And so that kind of comment I wish we could strike from the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, I think your question has got a point, but there's a lot of unnecessary comments, you know, there. You don't need those comments to gain your purpose, you know, by asking questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did -- let's let it to rest. Did your intelligence -- or security officer, Drago Nikolic, participate in killings personally?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, Drago Nikolic was not an intelligence officer. He was the chief of security and also assistant to the commander of the Zvornik Brigade for security. And as I've already said, Baljkovica, on the 15th, in the afternoon, I learnt that, yes, that was so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. He killed. It wasn't that he just merely ordered; he participated in killing innocent, harmless, human beings. Let's call it for what it is. Isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And the only difference between him and them is that they happened to be Muslim and he happened to be something other than Muslim?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, also, there is nothing from which you can look at or we can look at today that would verify whether in fact what Popovic was telling Nikolic was correct, if indeed, if indeed, Popovic told Nikolic: "Everybody knows about it, including your commander," that part.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure I understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you never called Popovic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at that period of time. Perhaps before or afterwards, but during that particular period, no, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You're in the eye of the storm. You're asking for help. You're reaching out to General Zivanovic because you need assistance to repel the 28th Division that is heading your way; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But when Nikolic gives you this information, which obviously, at least -- maybe it wasn't quite clear to you at that point, but obviously was going to consume a certain amount of your resources, you didn't reach out to call Popovic to verify whether in fact the information he had given to Nikolic was correct, particularly the part: Everybody knows about it, including the commander. That part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. This has been established three times. At this point I think it becomes a harassment of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: First of all, Your Honour, it seems -- I find it supremely ironic that the Prosecutor jumps up and objects at the moment when I'm trying to make a point. We established the fact that from Nikolic's point of view we cannot verify it. Now the question is on Popovic, because we don't know whether the conversation between Popovic was -- what it was. Did Popovic in fact say to Nikolic ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, the witness I think has answered this question, that he did not call Mr. Popovic at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And there's no way of verifying whether in fact Popovic had told Nikolic, on the night of the 13th: Everybody knows about it, including the commander. That part.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether anything exists, but what I knew, I said. Nikolic -- Drago Nikolic conveyed that to me, and to the best of my recollections, I told you what he told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you assumed, when he told you this, that everybody must know about it; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believed him, because he said that he was expecting a man to turn up who would inform him of the details in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, what I'm particularly focusing on the "everybody knew about it, including the commander," that part, because it seems rather peculiar, under the circumstances, that you would not reach out to try to locate your commander. So obviously you must have believed him and then maybe with the fatigue factor decided there's nothing more you can do, it's a fait accompli?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection to the form of the question. It was a statement, it had six parts in it, and it's not helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I agree with you that it's a compound question, but there's a point in this question. Maybe, Mr. Karnavas, you could rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You never checked that information to see whether the "everybody knows, including the commander" is actually a fact; that you never checked.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not check, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, the next thing you did do is provide some assistance in this operation that you had learned from your security -- your chief of security?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that. I said what my assistance consisted of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And we're going to talk a little bit about that, but not so much as to what the assistance was. But I do want to discuss how you deployed your military police prior to this. But before we get there, I want to show you a document, and it's been marked for identification purposes as D50. It's an interim combat report that was prepared by Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic. And the areas that I wish to focus on are on the second page, and the last two paragraphs, and going into the third page. But in Srpski, I believe, it's page number 3. I think it would begin with the second paragraph up there. But if you could look at that and the paragraph number 4, and if we can just discuss that for a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, in keeping with our normal practice, I believe -- I mean, I don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I will need more. I need several minutes for this, so I would rather --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please indicate how much time you still need to finish your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Oh, cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The entire cross?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I'm moving at a good clip, Your Honour, as you can see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And so probably the whole day. Well, it might be shorter. It might be shorter, but I don't want to box myself in to a particular time frame. But I will try to be as efficient as I possibly can, and I'll try to wrap it up by lunch-time. But I cannot guarantee that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, make your best efforts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: -- To finish it before the lunch-time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour. I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a break. We'll resume at a quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, we just have one matter to bring to the attention of the Trial Chamber, and in the form of a request. I have asked Mr. McCloskey if we could be provided a copy of the Obrenovic sentencing memorandum before I cross-examine Mr. Obrenovic. It was filed confidentially. We have not been provided a copy. I think it is very relevant and we would like to request the Court to go under the confidentiality ruling. We are all officers of the Court and we have signed a promise of confidentiality, but we would like to look at the sentencing memorandum before cross-examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. McCloskey, do you want to have a response?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I was just requested this a few minutes ago, and I really -- it's hard for me to respond at this point. I would like to review what was said, discuss with counsel. Fundamentally, I don't know if there's any big problem, but I think it bears a review.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. For the record, we were provided, upon our request, the Nikolic sentencing memorandum, so I do believe that in all fairness, the Jokic team should be entitled to that as well. So I just wanted to point that out when the Court makes its ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, Ms. Sinatra, you asked for that you be provided with that sentencing filings before your cross-examination, which means today. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So long as we've got your promise of the confidentiality, so long as we've got your promise of the confidentiality, I believe you'll be provided a copy of that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We signed those documents with the Prosecution at the beginning of the case, and I am an officer of the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So this document could be provided during the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karnavas, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Obrenovic, I'm told that -- maybe you have your speakers on too high. Your listening, there might be a -- for the translators, you may want to tune it down a bit, because there's an echo apparently. Okay. Now, we left off where I had provided you for your review what has been marked as D50 for identification purposes. Have you had a chance to look at it, Mr. Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe Ms. Sinatra may wish to object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I wish to object to this document on the grounds of lack of authenticity. It was translated from handwritten notes which have not been verified as being Commander Pandurevic's handwriting at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, since this document is introduced by Mr. Karnavas, Mr. Karnavas, can you shed some light on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, the light I could possibly shed is that, one, I received this document from the Prosecution, I received the translation from the Prosecution. From my understanding, it appears to be an accurate document, an authentic document, and pursuant to my knowledge of the events as they ensued, the document seems to be consistent with those events. So I have no reason to believe that it is not authentic, but we do have someone from the Zvornik Brigade. I can lay some foundational questions, which I was about to, and then if Ms. Sinatra has a further objection it could be noted for the record and then I could proceed with my questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. This document is a well-known document cited by Mr. Butler. The one that I have is a typed -- originally typed. I do not recall if we have a handwritten version. We may. But it was obtained in a search of the Zvornik Brigade, and as all the indicia, reliability appropriate for use in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I can verify, it is typed and it's in Cyrillic, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Ms. Sinatra, I think that, as I said before, that using a document and admission of the document is different matters, and at this moment we are going through this document, bearing in mind your objections to this document. And at a later stage, if the parties would like to tender this document into the evidence, at that time you have the full opportunity to reiterate your objections.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your cooperation. Mr. Karnavas, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Obrenovic, could you please tell us what this document is.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey -- I apologise. Mr. Karnavas, I think what you have supplied me with is a copy of an interim combat report from the command of the infantry brigade, dated the 18th of July, 1995. There are several pages to the document, three, in actual fact, and at the end it is signed by Commander Lieutenant Colonel Vinko Pandurevic, and I would say that that was initialed by him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, does that mean that you recognise the initial, Mr. -- Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic's?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said: It appears to be his, but I'm not ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, well, would this document appear to be an authentic document?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It appears to be that it is the copy of an authentic document, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And it is the practice of the Zvornik Brigade, as other brigades, to prepare interim combat reports, is it not, or was it not at the time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The interim combat reports were sent out according to need, as the name itself says, an interim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. Now, I had asked you if you could -- by the way, had you ever seen this document before meeting with your lawyers? In other words, did you see it at the time it was drafted, on or about the time, that is, on or about July 18, 1995?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I don't believe I saw it on the 18th, because on the 18th we were -- our time was taken up with practical matters. I think I saw it sometime around the 24th or after that date. Perhaps not this particular document, but from the war diary and copies from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'd ask you to focus on a particular section in this document, and I believe, if I'm correct, it's on page 3 of your document, which would be 00684886. I think that's the ERN number. And it's 2 on the English version. The second-to-last paragraph begins by stating: "We request that our appetites be adopted to realistic resources and possibilities." Do you see that portion? The paragraph immediately above paragraph number 4.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found that sentence, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. If you read that paragraph real quickly so we can discuss it.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. This paragraph would suggest that the Zvornik Brigade had been tasked to carry on combat activities to the point where perhaps their resources were being stretched to the maximum. Would that be a fair characterisation of what Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic is saying here?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. From the spring of 1995, the brigade was engaged in continuous combat, taking part in combat, and that's what that refers to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And could it possibly also refer to parts of the Zvornik Brigade, the two units that he had, being immediately tasked to go towards Zepa, when the situation remained fluid in the field with respect to the 28th Division?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we go to the next paragraph, number 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do we have this on the ELMO? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, it seems -- the second sentence says: "It is inconceivable to me that someone brought in 3.000 Turks of military age and placed them in schools in the municipality, in addition to the 7.000 or so who have fled into the forest. This has created an extremely complex situation and the possibility of the total occupation of Zvornik in conjunction with the force at the front. These actions have stirred up great discontent among the people and the general opinion is that Zvornik is to pay the price for the taking of Srebrenica." Now, the part that I wish to focus on is the beginning, where it says: "It is inconceivable to me" - that is Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic, commander of the Zvornik Brigade - "that someone brought in 3.000 Turks of military age and placed them in schools in the municipality," and so on and so forth. Does it not appear from this that he was taken aback, he was surprised at the fact that prisoners were brought into Srebrenica -- I mean into Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. It may appear that way at first glance, but that wasn't the actual situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let me rephrase it. From reading this sentence, it says: "It is inconceivable to me that someone brought in 3.000 Turks of military age and placed them in the municipality." What do you think he's saying here?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps I think this entire interim report was a consequence of a certain pressure put on the commander because of the opening up of the corridor I mentioned a few days ago, and this corridor had actually been forced. And as a consequence of this, he was trying to justify himself before the Main Staff and represent the entire situation as being extremely difficult, so that they would have to come to the conclusion that the corridor had to be opened, because he had done something that had not been approved by General Mladic, and this entire report is in fact an attempt to justify himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, do you think that Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic would have agreed to allow the 3.000 prisoners to come in, into Zvornik, while he had taken the cream of the Zvornik Brigade to go off to Zepa and leave you behind, facing the 28th Division? Do you think that that's conceivable?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic made the decision as to where he was to go or not. I don't think so. I think he received orders. General Krstic or Mladic or whoever it was issued orders, as it happens in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you were having a difficult time trying to figure out the strength of the 28th Division, do you think -- and you were there in Zvornik, do you think your commander, Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic, had greater knowledge of the situation, where you were situated, from where he was, and that is, on his way to Zvornik? Do you think that's possible?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What time period are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm referring to the 13th, the night of the 13th, that critical night. If you were uncertain of the situation and you were there, and he's on his way towards Zepa, surely you're not suggesting that he had greater knowledge about the 28th and how dangerous the situation was than you did.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, this is a compound question, but I will try to find my way in it. First of all, I don't know where Commander Pandurevic was exactly on the 13th, and therefore I can't say here is the proof that he was in such-and-such a place. I can only guess. Secondly, I told you where I was on the 13th and what information I had. All the commanders, starting from Mladic, to all the others who were in Bratunac, were involved in the Krivaja 95 operation, and they were all fighting the 28th Division. And all of them, like me, knew approximately how many men that division had. Suddenly, that division disappeared. In Potocari, they captured civilians, without any soldiers, and logically, when things calmed down, I asked the commander and I said: "Sir, where is the 28th Division? You found three old women in Srebrenica. Where has the division gone? You knew it would come to Zvornik." So what I'm getting at is that Pandurevic was not a naive soldier. He probably didn't know on what hill the 28th Division was, what stream it was crossing, but he knew that it was making its way in our direction. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say that he also knew their potential strength?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's hard to generalise. I think he knew roughly, on the 13th everybody knew, in the afternoon, about some of the prisoners, but perhaps he didn't know that there were 7.000 to 10.000 of them. He knew, however, that it was a considerable number, that there was a considerable force somewhere. He may not have known where exactly they were at what point of time, but everybody knew that they were somewhere in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. When did you begin asking for help? When did it become alarming to you to the point where you're reaching out and informing your higher commands that the situation was grave enough that you needed some help? Was it the 12th, the 13th? If the 13th, approximately when?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 13th, in the evening, you saw in that conversation General Zivanovic said that I should apply to the MUP, but they arrived only around midnight of the 13th, and that was only the Doboj Company. During the 14th, I intensified my requests, and then in the night of the 14th to the 15th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But I also recall you stating on direct examination that some of the information that you were getting, some of the advice that you were getting, seemed to be somewhat unrealistic, given the circumstances on the ground in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And this led you to believe -- which led you to believe - and I'm underscoring that - that -- well, let me put it crudely. They were more or less without a clue as to how dangerous it was for you and for the municipality in Zvornik; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In general terms, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, as you sit here today testifying under oath, you cannot verify to any degree of certainty that the commanders, or everybody, including your commander, were part of any decision making or planning or discussions with respect to the executions that took place, can you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I didn't say that you said it. I'm asking you the question. As you sit here today, is it not a fact that you cannot verify to any degree of certainty that the commanders, including your commander, were part of some decision-making process or part of the discussions with respect to these executions? That's the question.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can say is that on the 15th, as soon as Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic arrived, I told him the corridor -- what I have already testified to, and that's how it was. After the 17th, when we saw the men killed in Orahovac, on the spot -- I can't say anything about what happened before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me rephrase my question slightly better, and I apologise. It's my fault. On the night of the 13th, when you received that call, okay. So I'm focusing in that area. As you stand here today, you cannot verify to any degree of certainty that everyone, the commanders, including your commander, were part of any decision-making process or had knowledge of the executions that took -- that were to follow; isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. It needs to be broken down. Everyone, his commander. Those are all different people. I think it's a perfectly fair question, but it's unfair to ask it in that manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I agree with you. It's a fair question. But the issue is how to put your question, come across.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I'll ask the same question three different times, which means I take three times longer, Your Honour. I'm trying to be efficient, but very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: As you sit here today, you cannot verify to any degree of certainty that everyone was aware, on the night of the 13th, when you got that call, that the prisoners were going to be executed; isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, it's a fact that I knew only what Drago Nikolic had told me at the time, nothing more apart from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So the answer is -- so your answer is: You cannot verify to any degree of certainty that your commander knew, on the night of the 13th - I'm not talking about later on, but on the night of the 13th - when you get the call from Drago Nikolic, okay, you cannot verify to any degree of certainty that Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic knew of the plan, if there was such a plan, to execute the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat: I know nothing except for Drago Nikolic told me then. At the time, I thought that Drago Nikolic would not be playing games with such matters. It seemed impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, we're not asking -- again, I'm going to focus my question, this time with respect to Colonel Blagojevic, all right? As you stand here today, having looked at all of the documents, gone over them with your lawyers, all your conversations with the Prosecution and their investigators and what have you, you cannot state here today with any degree of certainty that on the night of the 13th, when you received the call from Drago Nikolic, that Colonel Blagojevic knew of any plan to execute the prisoners; isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, if I remember rightly, I never claimed anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I never suggested that you claimed. I'm not suggesting that you claimed it. I'm asking the question, okay? Because obviously you took Drago Nikolic's word. You accepted what he had -- what he represented. And now the question is: Years later, after you've looked at all of these documents and, and looking back, and having been in that situation, today, under oath, you cannot state with any degree of certainty that Colonel Blagojevic, on the night of the 13th, was aware of any plan to execute, or any order given by Mladic, to execute the prisoners; isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't swear to the night of the 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge, any knowledge, from all of the documents that you have -- because I'm not asking you to swear. We're talking about very limited issue of: Everybody knows, including the commander. Is there anything that you can pinpoint your finger on, that we could look at, touch, feel, smell, review, that would give us some certainty that your commander, or Colonel Blagojevic, on the night of the 13th knew of any order by General Mladic, if such an order existed, to kill the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The question was first Pandurevic, then Blagojevic. It's a fine question. I just wish the witness would be directed on which he's talking about, because it's impossible to answer those things all at once.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, well, well, I think Mr. Karnavas is asking about Mr. Blagojevic at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll focus on Mr. Blagojevic. Do you want me to restate the whole question again?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I'll try to repeat myself. As you sit here today, sir - it's not a trick question, but as you sit here today, you cannot show us any document that would give us any certainty that on the night of the 13th, Colonel Blagojevic knew of any order by Mladic to execute any prisoners?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I have not seen such a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I'll accept that and I'll move on, Your Honour. I apologise if I pressed you a little too much, but I'm trying to be certain on this. Okay. Let's move on to another topic, and now I want to focus you on the military police, but sort of in a different manner in which you were questioned on. As I understand it, that prior to the call from Drago Nikolic, the Zvornik Brigade military police, had been tasked by you to assist in or to partake in ambushes. Am I correct or am I off the path on this one?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're partly right, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me -- okay. All right. Help me out here. Help me out.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military police of the Zvornik Brigade was deployed up to that time in three ambushes, under my orders, and one traffic squad was sent to the Konjevic Polje crossroads, and this was ordered by the commander of the Drina Corps on the 12th. And the standard elements of the military police, under orders from Pandurevic and later Drago Nikolic, were in every infantry battalion. There were two military policemen from before, and then there were several policemen at the desk, at the detention unit. The lawyers from the military police were doing their job, and all these things that I've just said were not under my orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I believe you testified on -- it's October 2nd, October 2nd, 2003. And I'm quoting here from the transcript, on page 25, lines 1 through 3. You say: "A platoon from the military police company which had been deployed at that time I sent to the ambush" -- it says sear. It perhaps means rear. "And that they were there to go reconnaissance work at the canyon by the village." And it goes on, so on and so forth. Do you recall making that statement?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. So you actually had tasked them to assist in a combat operation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To carry out reconnaissance of the Drinjaca River canyon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, this is somewhat unconnected, but I want to, with the -- I would like to show you what has been premarked as D17/1 for identification purposes. I think you looked at it yesterday. And it is an order prepared by Colonel Blagojevic dated 5 July 1995. And perhaps you could help us out here a little bit.
